posts.cooked:
Hi,

I used relative path for the source file from the current working directory to create a soft link. It did create a link. But according to the screenshot below, it requires me to use the absolute path.

image2568×62 26.8 KB

Why is that? Does this mean it is advisable to use absolute paths for soft links?

Attaching the directory structure for reference.

.
└── project
    ├── bin
    │   ├── module1_hardlink.h
    │   └── module2_hardlink.so
    ├── docs
    │   ├── api
    │   └── manual
    ├── documentation -> ./project/docs
    └── src
        ├── module1
        │   ├── include
        │   │   └── module1.h
        │   └── lib
        │       └── module1.so
        └── module2
            ├── include
            │   └── module2.h
            └── lib
                ├── module1_symlink.so -> ./src/module1/lib/module1.so
                └── module2.so

Thanks!

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked:
Relative paths are equally valid as absolute paths when used in soft links. However there is a catch that you should remember when using relative paths in soft links. The relative path should be relative from the link’s location, not the current working directory, unlike all other commands.

You have also made that same mistake. The link should not be to ./project/docs as the link is already inside the project folder, it should be just docs

However, if you do that correctly, then relative path and absolute path both are equally valid. However, if using relative path it may become broken if you move the link.

This BPT is configured to accept only absolute path as you correctly pointed out, so here we should use absolute paths.

sayan:

Relative paths are equally valid as absolute paths when used in soft links.

Does this apply to hard links too?

posts.name: Sayan Ghosh
posts.cooked: It does not apply to hard links as hard links do not store the path, the path is used to resolve the file immediately by bash itself so relative path from cwd (not link) or absolute path both works
